items.prompt: Define profit.
items.canonical_answer: Profit is the surplus that remains when a business's total costs are subtracted from its revenue for a period. A positive surplus is a profit; a negative one is a loss.
marking_guidance: Precise meaning: the definition must relate profit to revenue less total costs over a period. Saying profit is "money made" without naming revenue and total costs is not a definition.

items.prompt: A Khomasdal bakery took N$9 800 from sales in June, while its ingredients, wages, rent and power came to N$10 300. Explain why the bakery made a loss rather than a profit.
items.canonical_answer: Profit depends on the gap between revenue and total costs, not on the size of revenue alone. Revenue for June was N$9 800, while total costs were N$10 300, so costs exceeded revenue by N$500: 9 800 - 10 300 = -500. A loss is what the calculation gives when total costs are the larger figure, because the business paid out more in earning its revenue than the revenue brought in. Sales were healthy; the relationship between the two figures was not.
marking_guidance: Reason: award for the because at the centre - profit is the comparison of revenue with total costs, so a business can sell steadily and still lose money.
Second reason: award for reading the given figures - total costs of N$10 300 against revenue of N$9 800 makes the loss, by N$500.

context.situation: a month of healthy sales at a loss

items.prompt: Explain the features of the way a profit is made.
items.canonical_answer: Profit comes from a comparison of two figures over a period, and its features are: revenue, the income from sales in the period; total costs, every cost of earning that revenue, from materials to rent; the subtraction of the second from the first, which yields a surplus or a loss; and the period itself, because profit is measured across a stretch of time such as a month or a year rather than at a single moment. What the comparison includes on each side is what decides the answer: subtract every cost and the surplus is profit; leave a cost out and the figure flatters the business.
marking_guidance: Features: award one mark for each element stated - revenue, total costs, the subtraction over a period - and one mark for developing what the comparison includes when a cost is left out.

items.prompt: Define retained profit.
items.canonical_answer: Retained profit is the part of a business's profit that is kept in the business after the owners have taken their share, rather than being paid out. It is an internal source of finance, available to fund the business's next plans without borrowing.
marking_guidance: Precise meaning: the definition must include the part of profit kept in the business after the owners' take-out. Naming profit alone, without the keeping, is not the definition.

items.prompt: A Gobabis machinery-repair business has just recorded its first yearly profit. Explain how this profit could lead to the business expanding, and how the expansion could then create new risks for the owners.
items.canonical_answer: Condition: if the owners keep most of the profit in the business rather than taking it out, they hold retained profit, an internal source of finance. Mechanism: because internal finance needs no lender's approval and carries no interest, the business can order new equipment or move to larger premises sooner than if it had to borrow, and the profit record itself makes outside finance easier to obtain if more is needed. Consequence: capacity rises, the business can serve more customers, and profit can grow again in later years - a gain for owners and for the workforce. The new risks follow from the same move: an expansion sized on one good year may prove too large if demand dips, because the extra premises and machines must still be paid for; and if the profit is still owed by customers on credit, the timing of the cash can lag behind the plan, so the owners should check the money is actually in hand before signing.
marking_guidance: Condition: the chain must start from the given position - a first profit - and be tied to the owners keeping it in. Mechanism: award for the how or the because - retained profit funds expansion without borrowing costs. Consequence: award for the effect - capacity, later profit, gains for the business and its workers - and for the risk side of the chain: an expansion can outgrow the demand behind it, threatening survival if the good year does not repeat.

context.situation: first profitable year, expansion under consideration

items.prompt: Ongwediva Car Wash made a profit of N$18 000 last year. The owner wants to open a second branch, which would cost about N$30 000 to set up. Explain what the profit figures mean for the owner's plan and what she should weigh before deciding.
items.canonical_answer: The context: the business can retain up to N$18 000 from the year, against a plan costing N$30 000, so retained profit could fund about three-fifths of the branch without borrowing. The reasoning: a record of profit makes the business a stronger prospect for a lender, because the figures show the first branch covering its costs, so a loan for the remaining N$12 000 is more likely to be offered than it would be to a business with no profit record - though the timing of payments should be checked, since profit is earned across the year while the set-up money is spent within weeks. Conclusion: the plan is realistic for this business provided the owner is confident the second branch can match the first; if she is not, opening smaller - two bays rather than a full branch - keeps much of the opportunity while risking less.
marking_guidance: Context: award for using this business's facts - N$18 000 of profit against a N$30 000 set-up cost. Reasoning: award for the link from the profit record to the funding of the plan, and to the check that the profit will be in hand when the money is spent. Conclusion: award a choice for this business that follows from the reasoning.

items.prompt: Explain the main elements of the importance of profit to a private-sector business.
items.canonical_answer: The importance of profit has four elements. Reward: profit pays owners for the risk they took in setting the business up, which is why private-sector owners accept the risk at all. Finance: the part of profit kept in the business becomes retained profit, an internal source of finance for development without borrowing. Signal: profit shows the business covering its costs, which tends to reassure customers, suppliers and anyone considering lending to it. Survival: sustained losses drain a business's funds, while profit rebuilds them, so profit matters to the objective of staying in operation. What all four share is a relationship between the business and its owners: private-sector owners invest to earn a return, and profit is that return.
marking_guidance: Elements: award one mark for each part - reward for risk, retained profit as finance, the signal profit sends, survival - and one mark for what the importance includes for the owners of a private-sector business specifically.

items.prompt: A learner writes: "A business that makes a profit never needs to borrow." Explain the error in this statement.
items.canonical_answer: The error is treating profit as if it covered every funding need, whatever the scale. In fact retained profit is one internal source, and it has three limits the statement ignores: the amount kept in may be smaller than the plan, because owners take part of the profit out; the timing may not match, since profit is earned across a period while a project's spending falls in a short window; and the profit is earned before the cash is in hand when customers buy on credit. The test that separates the ideas: ask whether the money for the plan is already in the business's account at the moment the bills fall due. If it is not, borrowing or another source is still needed, whatever the profit figure says.
marking_guidance: The error is named and corrected: in fact profit is one source and a limited one, wrongly treated as enough on its own.
Award the second mark for the test that separates the confused pair - whether the money is in the account when the bills fall due.

items.prompt: Define cash.
items.canonical_answer: Cash is the money a business holds and can spend at once: notes, coins and the balance in its bank account. It differs from profit, which is a surplus earned over a period; cash is about what can be paid today.
marking_guidance: Precise meaning: the definition must name money the business can spend at once, held as notes, coins and bank balance. Confusing cash with profit is precisely the error to avoid.

items.prompt: Explain the difference between profit and cash.
items.canonical_answer: The boundary: profit is the surplus of revenue over total costs, earned across a period; cash is the money the business actually holds and can spend now. The two differ because of timing and credit. A sale counts toward profit when it is made, whereas the cash from it arrives when the customer pays; a business can therefore be profitable in a month and still lack the cash to meet its payroll, and a business can hold cash - from a loan or savings - while making a loss. Both sides of the contrast matter: profitability asks whether the business earns more than it spends, and liquidity asks whether the money to pay this week's bills is there this week.
marking_guidance: Distinction: award for the boundary - profit is earned over a period whereas cash is held and spendable now - drawn on both sides with timing and credit.
Second award for showing each side alone misleads: profitable but cash-short, or holding cash while loss-making.

items.prompt: Explain the features that separate profit from cash.
items.canonical_answer: Four features separate them. Timing: profit is measured across a period, cash at a moment. Credit: revenue, and with it profit, is recorded when a sale is made, while cash waits for payment. Liquidity: paying this week's bills depends on cash, not on the profit figure. Source: cash can arrive without any profit being earned, as when an owner injects savings or a loan is received. Together the features mean a business judges its trading with the profit figure and its ability to pay with its cash position.
marking_guidance: Features: award one mark for each element - timing, credit, liquidity, source - and one mark for what the separation includes: profit judges trading performance, cash judges the ability to pay.

items.prompt: Define cost of sales.
items.canonical_answer: Cost of sales is the direct cost of the goods a business sells in a period: for a retailer, the buying price of the goods sold; for a manufacturer, the materials and direct labour that went into the units sold. It is the figure taken from revenue to reach gross profit.
marking_guidance: Precise meaning: the definition must tie cost of sales to the direct cost of the goods sold in the period. Listing a business's running expenses instead is not the definition.

items.prompt: Tsumeb Traders sold goods for N$46 000 in March. Those goods had cost N$27 600 to buy from suppliers. Calculate the gross profit for March.
items.canonical_answer: Formula: gross profit = revenue - cost of sales. Substitution: 46 000 - 27 600 = 18 400. Units: gross profit is measured in Namibian dollars, so gross profit for March is N$18 400. Interpretation: the N$18 400 is the trading margin for the month - the sum the business generated above the direct cost of its goods, from which it must pay its running expenses.
marking_guidance: Formula: award for stating gross profit = revenue - cost of sales.
Substitution: award for the working 46 000 - 27 600 = 18 400, in Namibian dollars as the currency of the figures.
Interpretation: award for saying what the N$18 400 means - the margin available to cover expenses - not for restating the subtraction.

items.prompt: A Rundu furniture store's income statement for last year shows revenue of N$400 000, cost of sales of N$240 000, gross profit of N$160 000, expenses of N$150 000 and profit of N$10 000. The owner says the store is doing well because its revenue is high. Explain whether the statement supports the owner's view.
items.canonical_answer: The context: the statement is internally consistent - 400 000 - 240 000 = 160 000 and 160 000 - 150 000 = 10 000 - and the profit of N$10 000 is small against revenue of N$400 000, a margin of about 2.5 per cent. The reasoning: revenue says little on its own, because almost all of it is consumed before profit appears - the cost of the goods takes N$240 000 and running expenses take N$150 000, so expenses alone absorb almost the whole gross profit. Conclusion: the statement does not support the owner's view as it stands; the store trades at a healthy gross margin of 40 per cent, but its expenses leave a thin surplus, so the more accurate reading is a business whose problem is expenses, not sales.
marking_guidance: Context: award for using the named facts of the statement - the N$10 000 profit against N$400 000 revenue, and the N$150 000 of expenses.
Reasoning: award for the link from the figures to the judgement - high revenue with high costs proves little.
Conclusion: award a supported choice: the view is not supported, or is at best partly supported, on the margins stated.

items.prompt: A Keetmanshoop supermarket's gross profit has stayed at N$90 000 a year, but its expenses have risen from N$60 000 to N$78 000. Explain how this change could affect the business and its owners over the next two years.
items.canonical_answer: Condition: where gross profit holds steady at N$90 000 while expenses rise, profit falls, because profit is gross profit after expenses. Mechanism: profit was 30 000 a year, because 90 000 - 60 000 = 30 000, and is now 12 000, because 90 000 - 78 000 = 12 000, so the surplus available to the owners has fallen by N$18 000, from about a third of gross profit to about a seventh. Consequence for the business: less retained profit means less internal finance for repairs, stock and price cuts, and the owners may respond by raising prices or trimming services, which can push shoppers toward competitors. Consequence for the owners: their return for risk shrinks even though trading is unchanged, which threatens the survival of the store if the rise in expenses continues.
marking_guidance: Condition: the chain must start from the given - steady gross profit, rising expenses. Mechanism: award for the because - profit is gross profit less expenses, so the rise in expenses goes straight through it. Consequence: award for the effect on the business - less retained profit for renewal - and a second consequence for the owners, whose return and the store's survival are both exposed if the trend continues.

items.prompt: Explain the main features of an income statement.
items.canonical_answer: An income statement records trading performance over a period, and its features, in the order they appear, are: revenue, the income from sales in the period; cost of sales, the direct cost of the goods sold; gross profit, the surplus of revenue over cost of sales; expenses, deducted next; profit, the surplus after every cost; and retained profit, the part kept in the business after the owners take out their share. What the statement includes is a subtraction story: each figure is the previous one less a cost, which is why the order cannot be shuffled.
marking_guidance: Features: award one mark for each element in its place - revenue, cost of sales, gross profit, expenses, profit, retained profit - and one mark for what the ordering includes: each line subtracts from the one above.

items.prompt: A learner writes: "Gross profit is the profit of the business." Explain the error in this statement.
items.canonical_answer: The error is stopping the subtraction halfway and calling the result profit. In fact gross profit is revenue less the cost of sales alone, whereas profit is what remains after expenses are deducted as well - rent, administration, marketing and the rest. The test that separates them: ask which costs were taken away before the figure was reached. A business with a healthy gross profit can still make a loss if its expenses are heavy, so the two figures answer different questions about the same period.
marking_guidance: The error is named and corrected: in fact gross profit subtracts the cost of sales alone, wrongly reported as the final profit.
Award the second mark for the test that separates the confused pair - which costs were taken away before the figure was reached.

items.prompt: Define what is meant by using an income statement in decision-making.
items.canonical_answer: Using an income statement in decision-making means reading its revenue, cost and profit figures to judge how the business performed and to choose between courses of action - continuing a product, adjusting a price, tackling a cost - based on the profit each choice would produce. The statement matters because its figures show where the surplus is being made or lost.

items.prompt: The latest income statement of a Walvis Bay cafe shows profit falling even though revenue is rising. Explain how such a statement could lead the owner to change prices, and how the change could damage the cafe.
items.canonical_answer: Condition: if the statement shows rising revenue with falling profit, the surplus is being squeezed between them, most likely by rising input or expense costs. Mechanism: because the owner reads where the figures are moving, the statement points to price - charging more per item rebuilds the margin without needing more customers, so the owner raises prices. Consequence: profit per sale rises at first, and revenue per customer rises with it. But the same move works on the customers too: some may switch to a cheaper competitor or come less often, because price is a strong influence on where people buy, so total sales can fall by more than the extra margin gained, leaving profit lower than before the change. For the business the risk is a smaller, quieter cafe; for the owners the risk is that the fix chosen from the statement made the problem worse.

items.prompt: Explain the features of profit calculations as a basis for business decisions.
items.canonical_answer: Profit calculations support decisions through four features. Comparability: reducing options to the profit each would produce lets unlike choices - two products, two prices, two branches - be set side by side. Level of detail: the calculation can be run for the whole business or for one product line, so a manager can find where the surplus is earned. Evidence over time: comparing periods shows whether profit is rising or falling and where the movement comes from. Conditionality: every projection is a forecast, so a decision based on the figures carries the assumption that demand and costs behave as expected - the features include a warning that the next period may not repeat the last.
marking_guidance: Features: award one mark for each element - comparability, level of detail, evidence over time, conditionality - and one mark for what the basis includes when the assumptions fail.

items.prompt: A learner writes: "Oshikango Electrical uses its income statement to find out in which months next year its bank balance will run short." Explain the error in this statement.
items.canonical_answer: The error is confusing an income statement with a cash-flow forecast. An income statement records trading performance over a period, usually one that has ended: revenue, cost of sales, gross profit, profit and retained profit. It counts a sale when it is made, even if the customer pays weeks later, so it shows profit rather than the money in the bank. A cash-flow forecast looks forward: it estimates the cash expected to come in and go out month by month, including loans received and capital put in by the owner, and so shows the expected bank balance at the end of each month. The test that tells them apart: ask whether the document is about profit earned over a past period or about cash expected in future months. Oshikango Electrical wants to know when its bank balance will run short next year, which is a question about the timing of future cash, so it needs a cash-flow forecast. An income statement can show a healthy profit for a year while hiding a month in which customers buying on credit have not yet paid.
marking_guidance: The error is named and corrected: in fact the months when the bank balance runs short are shown by a cash-flow forecast, not an income statement, which records profit over a past period.

A 6-mark answer states what an income statement records and when (revenue, costs and profit over a period, sales counted when made), states what a cash-flow forecast records and when (expected cash in and out, month by month, in the future), and applies the test - past profit or future cash - to Oshikango Electrical's question.

items.prompt: The manager of a Namibian tour company that made its first profit last year wants to add two vehicles to the fleet. Write several linked points for the manager: state two ways the profit helps the purchase plan and two risks that remain, each with a reason, and close with your recommendation for this business.
items.canonical_answer: Point: retained profit from the year is an internal source of finance, so part of the purchase can be funded without borrowing and the interest it would carry. Point: the profit record shows the business covering its costs, which makes any lender it approaches a more willing listener, because the figures lower the perceived risk. Risk: the profit is earned across the year while the vehicles are paid for at once, and if clients settle invoices late, the timing of the cash can fall behind the plan - profit and cash are not the same thing, so the manager should check the bank balance, not the profit figure, before committing. Risk: one good year may not repeat, because tourist numbers swing with the seasons and the wider economy, and vehicles bought against a single profitable year can weigh on the business in a quiet one. Recommendation: buy one vehicle from retained profit now and review the second after another profitable year, which keeps much of the gain while limiting what is at risk for the business.
marking_guidance: Point: award for each point stated, up to two per side. Reason: award for the because behind each - internal finance avoids borrowing costs, and the timing of cash lags profit earned. Context: award for applying each point to the tour company's situation rather than in the abstract.

items.prompt: Otavi Packaging made revenue of N$150 000 last year against total costs of N$141 000. This year revenue is N$144 000 and total costs are N$133 000. The directors are considering a price cut of 5 per cent to win larger orders, which they forecast would raise next year's revenue by 15 per cent and total costs by 9 per cent. Using the figures, consider whether the directors should go ahead with the price cut.
items.canonical_answer: The figures: profit last year was 9 000, because 150 000 - 141 000 = 9 000, a margin of 6 per cent of revenue. Profit this year is 11 000, because 144 000 - 133 000 = 11 000, a margin of about 7.6 per cent - trading is strengthening before any price decision. Under the forecast, next year's revenue would be 165 600, because 144 000 x 1.15 = 165 600, and total costs about 144 970, because 133 000 x 1.09 = 144 970, giving profit of roughly 20 630, because 165 600 - 144 970 = 20 630. Judgement: on the forecast the cut lifts profit from about N$11 000 to about N$20 630, so the directors should go ahead if they trust the forecast. Criterion: what decides it is the volume response the forecast assumes - customers buying enough more to outweigh the lower price per unit. Counterargument: the forecast is the directors' own; if customers do not respond, revenue falls by the 5 per cent cut while costs stay near N$133 000, and profit collapses to about N$3 800, because 144 000 x 0.95 = 136 800 and 136 800 - 133 000 = 3 800. Condition: the recommendation depends on the volume forecast and holds unless rivals match the cut or input costs rise faster than the 9 per cent assumed - a trial price for key customers first would test the response at little cost.
marking_guidance: Judgement: award for a clear recommendation on the price cut. Context: award for using the figures - the N$9 000 and N$11 000 profits and the forecast profit of about N$20 630 against about N$3 800. Criterion: award for naming what decides it - the volume response the forecast assumes. Counterargument: award for the case against - a cut without the volume response collapses profit to about N$3 800. Condition: award for the recommendation depending on stated conditions - rival pricing and the cost forecast.

items.prompt: Plan, without writing the full answer, a response to this 12-mark task: "A business that makes a profit is a successful business." Consider this view. Set out the paragraphs you would write, the judgement you would reach and the criterion that decides it, the case against your judgement, and the conditions the recommendation would depend on.
items.canonical_answer: Plan. Paragraph 1, define the terms: profit as revenue less total costs; success for a business judged against its objectives, which for a private-sector business include the owners' return but are rarely profit alone. Paragraph 2, the case for the view: profit is the reward for risk and a source of finance, so a business earning it covers its costs, can fund its future and is likely to hold the confidence of customers and suppliers. Paragraph 3, the case against: profit says nothing about cash - a profitable business can run out of money to pay this week's bills, because of the timing of credit - and it says nothing about the longer term, where success can be judged by survival, market share or the owners' other aims. Paragraph 4, judgement: the view holds only weakly; profit is the best single indicator available, but the criterion that decides the question is whether the profit is sustainable and matched by cash the business can reach. Recommendation conditional on: the business's objectives beyond profit, the strength of its cash position, and the period the profit was earned over.
marking_guidance: Judgement: the plan must state the verdict the answer would reach. Context: the plan must use facts about how profit and success are built - reward, finance, cash timing. Criterion: the plan must name what decides the verdict - sustainability and the cash position behind the profit. Counterargument: the plan must include the case against the view. Condition: the recommendation must depend on stated conditions - objectives, cash position, period.

items.prompt: Nyati Cycle Repairs opened in Otjiwarongo eighteen months ago. Its first full income statement shows revenue of N$96 000, total costs of N$88 000 and profit of N$8 000. The bank statement, though, shows N$1 200 in the account, with N$9 000 of wages due on Friday and most customers still owing for work completed in the month. The owner wants to spend N$6 000 on new tools next month. Analyse the position and recommend what the owner should do.
items.canonical_answer: Analysis: the income statement shows a business earning a surplus - N$8 000 of profit on N$96 000 of revenue - so the trading itself works. The bank statement shows the other half of the position: about N$1 200 of cash against N$9 000 of wages due on Friday, with most customers still owing. The two differ because of timing and credit: profit is earned when the repair is done, whereas the cash arrives when the customer pays, and the tools would spend money the business does not yet hold. Judgement: the owner should not buy the tools next month. Criterion: what decides it is the payroll - wages are a commitment a business misses at its peril, and a firm that misses them can lose its workers even while profitable, so paying Friday's wages from cash comes first. Counterargument: the tools might raise efficiency and profit faster; against that stands the risk that spending the last of the cash turns a profitable month into a failure to pay. Recommendation conditional on: collecting the money customers owe before any purchase, and revisiting the tools once the bank statement, not the income statement, supports them.
marking_guidance: Judgement: award for a clear recommendation on the tools. Context: award for using the facts - the N$8 000 profit beside N$1 200 of cash and N$9 000 of wages due. Criterion: award for naming what decides it - the payroll commitment and the timing gap between profit and cash. Counterargument: award for the case for the tools, weighed against the risk of spending cash the business needs. Condition: award for the recommendation depending on collecting what customers owe first.
